subject: British History
title: 10. The Edwardian Era and Rise of Labour

segments.text: This short period is the hinge between nineteenth-century liberal politics and twentieth-century mass democracy, welfare reform, and the modern party system — Labour’s emergence here permanently ends the old Liberal-Conservative two-party pattern.

Practise one analytical outline answering: “How did the People’s Budget crisis lead to a permanent change in the constitutional power of the House of Lords?”
Do not treat Edwardian politics as ending precisely in 1910 with Edward VII’s death; historians often use the term more broadly for the pre-1914 period.
Do not say the Parliament Act abolished the House of Lords; it restricted its legislative veto.
Do not assume early Labour immediately replaced the Liberals; that realignment took further decades.
The Labour Representation Committee was founded in 1900 and renamed the Labour Party in 1906.
Liberal governments after 1906 introduced old-age pensions (1908) and National Insurance (1911).
The People’s Budget of 1909 provoked a constitutional struggle with the House of Lords.
The Parliament Act 1911 reduced the Lords’ power to block most legislation permanently.
This era is the bridge from Victorian liberal politics to mass democracy, welfare reform, and the twentieth-century party system — frame every answer accordingly.
The Parliament Act 1911 is a genuinely major, if often underweighted, constitutional turning point directly comparable in significance to the 1832 and 1867 Reform Acts.
